1093.title: Purifying, growing
1093.hook: the word means both to purify and to grow
1093.howItsDone: Muslims who meet the conditions pay zakat as a set share of their wealth each year, and teachers describe it with Qur'an 9:103 as purifying the giver as well as helping the receiver.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer as rest: give us rest by it. Now a new pillar begins.

A gardener walks out with shears and starts cutting a healthy rosebush. Whole stems, buds still on them, onto the ground. Someone watching winces: you're ruining it. The gardener says, wait until spring. A cut in the right place, and the plant comes back fuller. Taking away is how it grows. One of the pillars of Islam is built on a word that does the same strange thing. It's usually translated as alms, or charity, or the poor-due. But the word carries two meanings at once. Today, zakat.
screen: `A GARDENER CUTS A HEALTHY ROSE.` → `TAKING AWAY, AND IT GROWS.` → `A PILLAR: ZAKAT.`

segments.voice: You met zakat back on day nineteen, as the pillar about money. Today, slowly, the word itself. First, it comes from a root, z-k-w, that the classical Arabic dictionaries give two senses for: to be pure, and to grow, to increase. Lane's Arabic-English lexicon lists both. So zakat is, in one word, a cleaning and a growing. Second, the Qur'an uses both together. In surah nine the Prophet ﷺ is told, in Pickthall's words: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Notice who is purified. Not the money. Them, the givers. The alms do something to the person who gives, not only to the one who receives. Third, the growing. The Qur'an pictures spending in Allah's way as a single grain that sprouts seven ears, with a hundred grains in every ear. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet ﷺ say that charity does not decrease wealth. On a calculator, that can't be right. The tradition is pointing at a different arithmetic, where what grows is blessing, and the giver. Fourth, why it's a pillar and not just a kind thing to do. Zakat isn't a mood of generosity. It's an obligation, measured and regular, with rules about who pays, how much, and to whom, and the next days walk through them one at a time. Underneath the rules sits this word. The rules give the amount; the word gives what it's for. Not how much is lost, but what this makes room for.

Zakat. A pillar of Islam: a set share of wealth given each year. From a root that means both to purify and to grow. Today's word.
Your line: giving makes it grow. In the verse, the giver is the one made clean. Tomorrow: who pays.

1094.title: Who pays
1094.hook: adult Muslims with wealth above the threshold for a full lunar year
1094.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings pass the threshold and have been held a year work out their zakat once a year, and those unsure of their school's rules, for example on a child's savings, ask a scholar or a zakat body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zakat: a word that means to purify and to grow. Today, who pays it.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal is packing for Yemen. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is sending him to teach, and before he leaves, he gets his instructions, in order. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. First, call the people to the testimony. If they accept that, teach them the prayers. And if they accept that, tell them Allah has made a charity obligatory on them, taken from their rich and given back to their poor. From their rich, to their poor: in a handful of words, the answer to a question that sounds simple and isn't. Who actually pays zakat?
screen: `MU'ADH, PACKING FOR YEMEN.` → `TESTIMONY, THEN PRAYER, THEN ZAKAT.` → `FROM THEIR RICH, TO THEIR POOR.`

segments.voice: First, it's a duty for Muslims. The Qur'an sets it right beside the prayer. In surah two, in Pickthall's words: "Establish worship, pay the poor-due, and bow your heads with those who bow." Zakat is part of the practice of Islam, so it's asked of Muslims, not of their neighbors. Second, it's asked of the rich, in the Prophet's sense. Not a millionaire: someone whose wealth passes a set line, the threshold, which gets its own day tomorrow. Below that line, nothing is owed. A person who barely has enough is one of the people zakat is meant to reach, not one it's taken from. Third, the wealth has to sit. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says no zakat is due on wealth until a year has passed over it. Money that comes in and goes straight back out to rent and groceries isn't what's counted. What stays is. It's a yearly reckoning, not a toll on every paycheck. Fourth, the hard edge: who counts as an adult owner? Here the schools of law differ, and say so plainly. On savings held by a child, the Hanafi school says no zakat is due. Other schools say it is due, and a guardian pays it from the child's wealth. Shia jurists have their own rulings again. Nobody here is ranked; each answer comes with its own reasons. Put together, the picture is narrower than people sometimes assume. Not everyone pays, and not on every dollar. A Muslim, past the line, on wealth that stayed a year, gives a share.

If you're Muslim, those questions are the start of working out your zakat. If not, they're still a gentle way to see what you've been keeping, with no judgment.

1095.title: The threshold
1095.hook: the value of about 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver
1095.tomorrow: Two and a half per cent
1095.howItsDone: Muslims check the current nisab, published by mosques and zakat organizations from the price of gold or silver, before working out whether zakat is due on their savings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who pays: a Muslim past the line, on wealth held a year. Today, the line itself.

A brass scale on a market stall. On one side, a little heap of silver coins. On the other, a weight. The trader adds a coin, then another, and watches the beam. For a long time nothing happens. Then one more coin, and the beam tips. Before that coin, the heap is just what someone has. After it, the heap has crossed a line, and something is asked of it. Zakat works with a line like that. Fall short, and nothing is due. Reach it, and a share belongs to someone else. The line has a name: nisab.
screen: `A SCALE, A HEAP OF SILVER.` → `ONE MORE COIN, AND IT TIPS.` → `THE LINE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Nisab is the minimum, the amount wealth has to reach before zakat is owed on it. Below it, you're not counted among the rich in the sense of yesterday's hadith. First, where the line comes from. The hadith collections give it in the coins and goods of the Prophet's own day. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says no charity is due on less than five measures of silver, on fewer than five camels, or on less than five loads of grain or dates. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud gives the coins: on two hundred silver dirhams, five dirhams are due; on gold, nothing until it reaches twenty dinars, and then half a dinar. So the line isn't a fixed dollar figure. It's a weight of metal, a number of animals, a load of harvest, things you could see and hold. Second, the line today. Nobody's savings sit in dirhams now, so modern scholars and zakat bodies turn those coins into weights of gold and silver, then into money at today's price. The figure moves as gold and silver move, which is why it's looked up rather than memorized. Third, the honest question: gold or silver? The two lines no longer match in value. Some scholars say to use the lower of the two, so more wealth is counted and more reaches the poor. Others say to use gold's line, especially for savings held in money. Both come with reasons, and people follow the scholars they trust. Fourth, the point underneath. There's a floor. Below it, a person is protected. Above it, a share is owed.

Then picture the other side, what's left after needs, and without counting, notice whether it feels like a lot, a little, or nothing at all. The line is drawn so that need comes first.
Nisab. The threshold: the minimum wealth before zakat is due, first given in silver, gold, camels and grain. Today's word.
Your line: the line of wealth. Need comes first; the share comes after. Go gently.

1096.title: Two and a half per cent
1096.word: Two and a half per cent
1096.howItsDone: Muslims who owe zakat on money and savings give one fortieth, two and a half percent, of what they hold above the nisab, once a year, some using a mosque's or charity's zakat calculator.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nisab: the line wealth must reach before zakat is owed. Now, above it, how much?

Forty dates in a bowl, counted out by hand onto a plate. Thirty-nine go back to be eaten, shared, saved. One, just one, is set apart on the edge of the plate. That's the whole share. When people first hear zakat described as a pillar of the faith, a duty beside the prayer, some expect it to be heavy. A tenth, a quarter, half. Then comes the number, and it's small. Small enough to keep doing, every year, for a whole life. One coin out of forty: two and a half percent.
screen: `FORTY DATES IN A BOWL.` → `ONE SET APART.` → `SMALLER THAN SOME EXPECT.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In Sahih al-Bukhari there's a letter Abu Bakr wrote setting out the rules of zakat, and for silver it gives the share as rub' al-'ushr. A quarter of a tenth. Take a tenth, then a quarter of that, and you have one fortieth: two and a half percent. Second, the same share in coins. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud has the Prophet ﷺ say to bring a quarter of a tenth, one dirham from every forty. And the threshold you met yesterday says it the same way: on two hundred dirhams, five. Two hundred divided by forty is five. The numbers in these reports agree with each other. Third, what it's charged on. Not on income as it flows in, and not on everything you own. On saved wealth above the line, held a year: cash, savings, gold and silver, goods for trade. Teachers of the law don't count your home, the clothes you wear, or the car you drive to work in the same way, and a later day looks at the categories one by one. Fourth, why such a small share might be the point. It's something a person can give every year without being ruined by it, and the people who receive it can count on it coming, year after year. Small, steady, and owed. Which is harder than it sounds. Anyone can be generous once.

Two and a half percent. Rub' al-'ushr, a quarter of a tenth: one fortieth of saved wealth above the threshold. Today's word.

1097.title: The year
1097.hook: zakat is due when wealth has been held a full lunar year
1097.howItsDone: Muslims who pay zakat keep a yearly zakat date by the Islamic lunar calendar, some fixing it in Ramadan, and on that day total their zakatable wealth above the nisab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two and a half percent: one in forty, a quarter of a tenth. Today, the clock zakat runs on.

On the evening the new moon is first seen, someone steps outside, looks low on the horizon, and finds it: a thin silver line, barely there. A month has begun. Muslims have watched for that line for the start of Ramadan and the days of Hajj. It's also the clock for something less famous. Money in a savings account doesn't announce when zakat is due on it. No bill comes in the mail. The only reminder is the moon going around, month after month, until a whole year of moons has passed over what you hold. The word for that year: hawl.
screen: `A THIN SILVER LINE AT DUSK.` → `A MONTH HAS BEGUN.` → `A YEAR OF MOONS: HAWL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, with a similar one in at-Tirmidhi, says that no zakat is due on wealth until the hawl, the year, has passed over it. Wealth has to stay with you a full year before it's counted. Money that arrives and leaves in a season isn't. Second, which year. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "the number of the months with Allah is twelve months", and elsewhere calls the new moons fixed times for people. The Islamic calendar follows those moons, so zakat's year is a year of moons. And because the moon's year and the sun's don't line up, a zakat date fixed by the moon slides earlier on a wall calendar from one year to the next. Third, the exception. A harvest doesn't wait for a year. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due of their crops on the day of the harvest, and a later day on this path is about that. Fourth, the date itself. Some Muslims set it to the day their wealth first crossed the threshold, and count a year of moons from there. Some choose a day in Ramadan, so their giving falls in that month. And the schools of law differ on what happens if savings dip below the line partway through the year, so people ask a scholar they trust. What these answers share is a date: one day a year when the whole of what you hold gets looked at, honestly, and a share goes out.

When one feels like a day you'd actually keep, as your zakat date or, if zakat isn't yours, a day for looking honestly at what you have, let it stay.

1098.title: Gold, trade, crops, herds
1098.hook: zakat on cash and gold, trade goods, harvests and livestock, each with its rule
1098.howItsDone: Muslims add up their zakatable wealth by category, cash and gold, trade stock, crops, livestock, and follow their school of law on questions such as worn jewelry, leaving out the home, car and personal belongings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hawl: the year of moons that wealth must be held. Today, what gets counted on that day.

Four neighbors in an old market town. A shepherd, with a flock on the hills. A shopkeeper, with shelves of cloth waiting to be sold. A farmer, with a field of wheat turning gold. And a woman with gold coins saved in a box under the bed. Each might owe zakat by the end of the year. But you can't take a fortieth of a sheep, and you can't wait a year on a harvest that will rot. So zakat doesn't treat wealth as one heap. It sorts it, starting with the one that shines.
screen: `A SHEPHERD, A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A FARMER, A BOX OF GOLD.` → `WEALTH THAT DOESN'T LOOK ALIKE.`

segments.voice: First, gold and silver, and the money that now stands in for them. The Qur'an speaks hard words in surah nine about those who hoard gold and silver and don't spend it in the way of Allah. Wealth kept still, in a box, is wealth zakat plainly reaches: one fortieth, once a year, above the line. Modern scholars put cash and bank savings here too. Gold jewelry worn by a woman is where the schools of law differ: the Hanafi school counts it, and other schools, in general, don't count jewelry kept for wearing. Second, trade. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says the Prophet ﷺ commanded that charity be paid on what is prepared for sale. So the shopkeeper's shelves count, valued at the zakat date as if they were money; scholars don't count the shelves themselves, the shop, the scales. Third, crops. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due on the day of the harvest. No waiting a year, and a different share; tomorrow is that day. Fourth, herds. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr's letter of zakat sets out shares for camels and sheep, counted by heads, so a shepherd gives animals, not fractions. And what isn't counted? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says no charity is due from a Muslim on his horse or his slave, the things a person kept for his own use. Scholars take from it that your home, your car and your clothes are not zakat wealth. Underneath all four: zakat looks at wealth that sits or wealth that grows, and leaves alone what you live with.
screen: `GOLD, SILVER, AND MONEY.` · `WHAT IS PREPARED FOR SALE.` · `CROPS, ON THE HARVEST DAY.` · `HERDS, COUNTED BY HEADS.` · then, large: `EACH WEALTH HAS ITS SHARE.`

1099.title: The harvest's tenth
1099.hook: a tenth of rain-watered crops, a twentieth of irrigated ones
1099.howItsDone: Muslim farmers whose harvest passes the threshold give a tenth of rain-fed crops and a twentieth of irrigated crops at harvest time, following the hadith of Ibn Umar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four kinds of wealth: gold, trade, crops and herds. Today, the crops.

Two fields, side by side, the same wheat in each. On the first, the farmer did almost nothing for the water. Clouds came over, rain fell, the ground drank, and the wheat came up. On the second, the farmer had to work for every drop: a well, a bucket, an animal turning a wheel, hour after hour. Harvest day comes for both. Same crop, same weight in the barn. Does the second farmer owe the same as the first? The answer in the hadith is no, and the reason is in the sky.
screen: `TWO FIELDS, THE SAME WHEAT.` → `ONE RAIN-FED, ONE HAND-WATERED.` → `DO THEY OWE THE SAME?`

segments.voice: First, the rule. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar, says that on what is watered by the rain or by springs, or draws its own water, the share is a tenth. On what is watered by drawing water, the share is half a tenth. A tenth, or a twentieth. The Arabic word for that tenth is 'ushr. Second, the reason, as scholars explain it. The first farmer's water came free, from the sky. The second paid for his, in labor and cost. So the share follows the gift: where more was simply given, more is given back. That's why your line is rain's share. The extra in the first field's due is, in a sense, the rain's part. Third, the timing. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due on the day of the harvest. No year to wait. And a threshold applies here too, given in loads of grain in the same report you met with the nisab. Fourth, set this week's pieces side by side. Zakat, the word that means to purify and to grow. Who pays: from their rich, to their poor. The threshold, below which a person is protected. One in forty for savings. The year of moons. Four kinds of wealth. And today, the field: a tenth or a twentieth, depending on the rain. Read together, the rules ask one question in different ways: what was received, and how much of it came without anyone's doing?
screen: `A TENTH, OR HALF A TENTH.` · `THE SHARE FOLLOWS THE GIFT.` · `GIVEN ON THE HARVEST DAY.` · `THIS WEEK, ONE PICTURE.` · then, large: `RAIN'S SHARE.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, when the Prophet ﷺ saw rain, he would ask for it to be a beneficial rain: allahumma sayyiban nafi'an. If you pray, you can say those words now, or simply alhamdulillah. If you don't, remember the last rain you heard, the sound on a window, the smell of the street afterward, and follow it into soil, into wheat, into the bread you ate this week.
The harvest's tenth. 'Ushr: a tenth of rain-watered crops, a twentieth of crops watered by labor, given on the harvest day. Today's word.
Your line: rain's share. Next, the other side of the ledger: who receives it. A week of zakat, done.
